item.title: Debt Desk — Debt Desk Morning Brief for July 20, 2026
item.description: Tropical Depression Two, Texas flood cleanup, a first-ever Justice Department move into a dormant deportation court, and a widening produce recall lead the national morning brief before Debt Desk turns to the latest verified Treasury and SOFR prints, selective CRE execution, active multifamily capital, agency and CMBS signals, and one thing to watch for Monday, July 20, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
It is Monday, July 20th, and this is Debt Desk.

National

Let’s start with the national morning brief, because the country is opening this week with a mix of weather risk, legal escalation, and a food-safety story that has moved well beyond a single restaurant chain.

The first story is really two linked weather stories now. South and Central Texas are still in cleanup mode after last week’s flooding, but the weather risk has not fully cleared the map. The Associated Press reported over the weekend that the flooding killed at least two people, triggered hundreds of rescues, and damaged roads, bridges, homes and local business corridors across a broad stretch of the state. Now, as of Monday, July 20, the National Hurricane Center says Tropical Depression Two is lingering near the northern Gulf Coast and could bring more heavy rain along the coast and into parts of the region in the days ahead. That matters because once a market shifts from rescue into cleanup, even moderate additional rain becomes more disruptive than it would have been a week earlier. Crews are trying to restore access, insurers are beginning to size losses, and small businesses are trying to figure out whether they can reopen. So the Texas story is no longer just about dramatic weather footage. It is an infrastructure story, a municipal-stress story, and for lenders and investors, an early read on how quickly damaged local economies can normalize.

The second story is the Justice Department’s decision to activate the Alien Terrorist Removal Court for the first time since Congress created it in 1996. AP reported today, July 20, that the administration filed its first petition into that dormant court and that the judge immediately asked for more information after an initial hearing. The legal details matter, but the broader signal matters more. This is a reminder that the administration is still searching for harder-edged immigration tools and is willing to test little-used authorities if it thinks traditional channels are too slow or too exposed. That does not directly move a swap rate this morning, but it does add to the sense that Washington is operating in a more experimental, more confrontational posture. Markets do not ignore that kind of shift forever, especially when it shapes labor, enforcement risk, and political noise.

The third story is food safety, and it widened materially in the last twenty-four hours. AP reported Sunday, July 19, that Taylor Farms voluntarily recalled iceberg lettuce products shipped to 27 states after federal investigators tied cyclospora illnesses to lettuce served at Taco Bell in five states. That is important because the story has moved from one branded point of sale to a broader supply-chain issue. Once a recall jumps into multiple states and multiple product codes, it becomes a confidence story as much as a public-health story. Consumers pull back first, then operators start auditing sourcing, and then distributors and landlords start watching foot traffic and tenant performance more carefully if the problem lingers. It is not systemically important on its own, but it is another example of how a concentrated operating problem can spread nationally in very little time.

The fourth story is the smoke story, which is easing but not finished. AP reported Sunday that thunderstorms were expected to clear much of the wildfire smoke that had hung over the Northeast just in time for major outdoor events, but the last few days made clear that this is not a fringe environmental headline anymore. Air quality disruptions already hit sports schedules, outdoor activity, and basic day-to-day operating conditions across large East Coast and Midwest markets. Even if the haze improves this morning, the practical lesson remains the same: wildfire smoke is now a recurring business interruption risk, not a once-in-a-summer anomaly. It affects consumer behavior, outdoor labor, event economics, and even simple assumptions about when a city is fully open for business.

So the national setup for Monday is pretty straightforward. Texas is recovering while still exposed to additional rainfall risk. Washington is testing a new legal lane on immigration. The produce recall story is broader and messier than it first looked. And the smoke may be thinning, but the operating lesson from it is not going away. That is the backdrop for the debt conversation this morning.

Debt Desk

Now let’s turn to Debt Desk.

The first anchor is rates, and the numbers are verified. As of this Monday morning run, the latest official Treasury close is Friday, July 17. The curve closed at 3.80 percent on the 2-year, 3.92 percent on the 5-year, 4.00 percent on the 10-year, and 5.00 percent on the 30-year, according to the U.S. Treasury. The latest official SOFR print is 3.62 percent for July 16, according to the New York Fed.

That curve is worth sitting with for a minute, because the shape matters as much as the level. The front end has come in enough to keep shorter-duration fixed-rate debt and floating-rate structures alive, but the long end is still doing real damage to proceeds once you layer on lender spread, reserves, and structure. A 10-year at 4 percent is not a crisis print. A 30-year at 5 percent still feels heavy, especially for borrowers who need a full-term certainty story and do not have the cushion to absorb a wider all-in coupon. In plain English, money is more workable than it was when both the curve and spreads were punishing borrowers at the same time, but it is still not easy. That is why five-year money, hybrid structures, and transitional executions continue to matter so much.

That also helps explain why lender behavior is still segmented rather than broadly reopened. Banks can lend, but they do not have to pretend they are hungry across every product type. Life companies can still stay selective because long-duration capital remains valuable and the long bond is giving them cover to demand discipline. CMBS is available, but only where the collateral is clean enough to survive securitized scrutiny. And debt funds remain relevant because a lot of borrowers still need speed, flexibility, or tolerance for business-plan complexity that traditional lenders do not want to warehouse.

You can see that in the latest office-adjacent financing tape. Commercial Observer reported on July 17 that Hudson Bay Capital provided a $60 million bridge refinance for the Bell Works Fort Monmouth campus in Tinton Falls, New Jersey. This is not a generic office story. It is a repurposed mixed-use campus story with visible leasing momentum, occupancy around the high-eighties, and a headline tenant narrative anchored by Jersey Mike’s planned headquarters move. That distinction matters. Capital is still not broadly saying yes to office. It is saying yes when the sponsor can show that the property has already crossed the hard part of the bridge from obsolete space into a functioning mixed-use ecosystem with cash flow and a credible next chapter.

Bank balance-sheet tone remains selective as well. Trepp’s latest CRE debt work, highlighted this past week, shows overall debt growth improving, but with a very important split under the surface. The median bank is still adding CRE exposure, including some construction balances, while the largest banks continue pulling back enough to keep the aggregate picture restrained. That is the part borrowers need to hear clearly. There is debt available, but a few successful deals do not equal a broad reopening of construction appetite. If you are bringing a bank a relationship deal with good deposits, low leverage, and a clean sponsorship story, you have a lane. If you are asking for higher-leverage speculative exposure, the lane is still much narrower.

CMBS is telling a similar story. Trepp’s June delinquency data showed the headline CMBS delinquency rate improving to 7.35 percent, but that better headline sits next to continuing stress in the workout pipeline and elevated distress across major markets. Commercial Observer’s recent CRED iQ coverage showed overall CMBS distress among the 25 largest U.S. metro areas at 12.7 percent in May, with much sharper pain in certain office-heavy metros. So the right read is not that CMBS has turned easy. The right read is that the market is open for assets that can handle hard underwriting, while problem assets are still very much a servicing and maturity story.

That is why execution tone today still breaks out pretty cleanly by lender type. Banks want relationship business and defendable leverage. Life companies want durable income and minimal narrative risk. CMBS wants collateral that can travel well and survive secondary-market scrutiny. Debt funds want to be paid for complexity, transition, or time-sensitive closings. None of that is especially new, but the current curve is not forcing those lines to blur. If anything, it is keeping them in place.

Multifamily remains the deepest pool for real activity, and the last several days reinforced that from a few different angles at once. Commercial Observer reported July 17 that Ponce Bank provided $50 million of construction financing for two contiguous apartment buildings in Canarsie totaling 198 units. The deal closed July 13, and a portion of the units will qualify for New York’s 485-x tax-abatement program. That matters because it shows where construction credit still clears: apartments, policy support, a local housing-supply argument, and a basis lenders can defend without getting heroic. Construction money is still selective, but it is absolutely not absent when the story lines up.

Affordable housing capital also stayed active. Commercial Observer reported July 17 that Greystone Real Estate Capital closed its second affordable housing development fund at $137 million of LIHTC equity, aimed at nearly 2,000 units across 20 properties in nine states. That is not just an equity headline. It is a credit signal. Institutional capital is still willing to fund affordable housing at scale because the policy framework, tenant demand, and mission alignment remain easier to explain than a lot of market-rate development risk. For the multifamily stack overall, that means affordability continues to act as both a social objective and a capital-market advantage.

There was also a meaningful CMBS print inside multifamily. Commercial Observer reported July 17 that Citi priced an $816.9 million multifamily-only conduit transaction backed by 27 five-year interest-only loans, the largest single-bank-contributed multifamily-only conduit deal since the global financial crisis. That matters for two reasons. First, it tells you investor demand for apartment collateral remains real, not theoretical. Second, it reinforces how much the securitized market still prefers product types with stable cash flow and a simpler credit story. That deal does not mean every apartment borrower gets a wide-open conduit lane, but it does say the market will reward clean multifamily pools with sharper execution than many other property types can get right now.

Agency activity remains part of the stabilizing picture too. Freddie Mac’s official multifamily certificates calendar shows its K-1811 conventional fixed 10-year deal scheduled for announcement the week of Monday, July 20, with projected issuance size around $1.1 billion. That is not a final priced transaction yet, but it is still useful because it shows the agency securitization machine remains active and visible right into this week. In a market where borrowers care about dependable exits, that steady agency pipeline matters. Fannie Mae’s platform message remains similar. Its multifamily business continues to emphasize DUS execution, affordable housing, and green financing as the cleanest lanes for steady liquidity.

Trepp’s latest agency credit numbers back that up. Its July 17 update showed total securitized agency multifamily delinquency at just 0.47 percent in May, with Fannie Mae at 0.24 percent, Freddie Mac at 0.87 percent, and Ginnie Mae, FHA, and HUD at 0.51 percent. Freddie still runs somewhat higher, but the broader point is stability. Agency credit is not flashing stress in a way that would force a change in lender posture. It is still one of the cleanest parts of the broader CRE credit picture.

On HUD and FHA specifically, the freshest headline this morning is not a brand-new policy announcement. The more important read is that the federally backed multifamily channel still looks stable in the data, and that matters because it helps preserve confidence in the deeper affordable and workforce-housing lane even when private construction lending remains selective. In this market, no bad surprise from HUD or FHA-backed credit is itself useful information.

The concise markets snapshot this morning is this. The latest verified Treasury close is 3.80 percent on the 2-year, 3.92 percent on the 5-year, 4.00 percent on the 10-year, and 5.00 percent on the 30-year. The latest verified SOFR print is 3.62 percent. Bank appetite is better than it was, but large banks still are not broadly embracing construction risk. Office debt is getting done mainly where the repositioning story is already real. CMBS is functioning, but only for collateral that can stand up to tough underwriting. Multifamily remains the strongest lane, especially where affordability, agencies, or clean securitization fit are involved.

One thing to watch this week is whether multifamily liquidity keeps broadening from multiple directions at once. If we keep seeing apartment construction loans, affordable-housing equity raises, agency securitization, and multifamily-only conduit execution all show up together, then the right read is that lenders are extending comfort beyond just one narrow lane of apartment credit. If that follow-through stalls, then the market is still clustering around the single easiest collateral to defend rather than truly reopening.

The takeaway for this Monday is straightforward. Nationally, the week starts with live weather risk in Texas, a sharper legal posture out of Washington, a broader-than-expected food recall, and another reminder that environmental disruptions can hit major markets fast. In Debt Desk, the market is open, but it still rewards specificity. Borrowers can get debt, but the cleanest executions are still going to assets lenders already trust, capital stacks they can explain to committees, and business plans that do not depend on optimism carrying the underwriting. That remains most true in multifamily, selectively true in high-conviction adaptive-reuse office, and much less true anywhere the story still needs to be rescued after closing.

It is Sunday, July 19th, and this is Debt Desk.

National

Let’s start with the national morning brief, because the backdrop this weekend is a mix of cleanup, public-health disruption, and a federal policy posture that is getting more assertive in very visible ways.

The biggest continuity story is still Texas, but the angle has shifted. The Associated Press reported on July 18 that catastrophic flooding across South and Central Texas had killed at least two people, forced hundreds of rescues, damaged roads and bridges, and left communities from Uvalde outward trying to figure out what normal even looks like after days of relentless rain. That matters because the real economic impact of a flood rarely shows up in the first headline. It shows up when stores stay closed, medicine is hard to find, bridges stay offline, and families start counting what was lost inside homes and small businesses. So this is not just a weather story this morning. It is now an infrastructure, insurance and local-credit story, and it will stay that way into the coming week.

The second story is the air itself across the Northeast. AP reported this morning, July 19, that thunderstorms were expected to clear much of the wildfire smoke that has drifted in from Canada and Minnesota, after haze pushed into major East Coast markets and turned parts of the region gray for days. The improvement is meaningful, but it does not erase what the last stretch has shown. Wildfire smoke has become an operating condition, not just an environmental headline. It can change event planning, outdoor work, travel comfort, public-health guidance and consumer behavior in real time. Even when the air improves, the lesson for businesses and local governments is the same: this kind of disruption is showing up more often, and it does not respect regional boundaries.

The third story is out of Washington, where AP reported today that the Justice Department has activated the Alien Terrorist Removal Court for the first time since Congress created it in 1996. The court had never been used until the administration filed a petition on Wednesday, and the judge overseeing the matter has already asked the government for additional information after an initial hearing. The immediate significance is legal and procedural, but the broader significance is political and institutional. It tells you the administration is still looking for harder-edged immigration tools and is willing to test dormant authorities if it thinks the existing system is too slow or too exposed to public process. Markets are not repricing office loans because of one immigration court filing, but they do register when federal enforcement posture becomes more aggressive and more experimental.

The fourth story is a consumer health story with national reach. AP reported today that federal investigators traced lettuce served at Taco Bell locations in five states to a cyclospora outbreak. That is not on the same scale as a national disaster or a major policy fight, but it does matter because it hits a lot of the same themes that keep showing up across the economy right now: supply-chain quality control, public confidence, and how quickly a localized problem becomes a multi-state issue once a large national brand is involved. For consumers it is a practical warning. For operators it is another reminder that even an otherwise stable summer demand backdrop can be interrupted by one contamination event.

So the national setup this Sunday is pretty clear. Texas is moving from rescue into a long cleanup. The smoke story may be easing, but it is still a live sign of environmental disruption spilling into daily business. Washington is testing more aggressive legal machinery on immigration. And public-health risk has jumped back into the headlines through a national restaurant chain. That is the atmosphere borrowers, lenders and investors are walking into today.

Debt Desk

Now let’s turn to Debt Desk.

The first anchor is rates, and the numbers are verified. As of this Sunday morning run, the latest official Treasury close is Friday, July 17. The curve closed at 4.18 percent on the 2-year, 4.28 percent on the 5-year, 4.55 percent on the 10-year and 5.06 percent on the 30-year. The latest official SOFR print is 3.62 percent for July 16, according to the New York Fed.

That curve still tells the same basic story, but it is worth slowing down on the shape because the shape matters more than the headline. The front end is no bargain, yet it is restrained enough to keep shorter fixed-rate structures and floating-rate executions in the conversation. The long end is the heavier part of the stack. A 10-year in the mid-fours is workable in theory, but the 30-year above 5 percent keeps long-duration money expensive once lender spread, reserves and structure get layered in. In plain English, borrowers still are not choosing between cheap money and expensive money. They are choosing between manageable pain and more durable pain, and that keeps five-year thinking very alive.

That also explains why lender behavior still feels segmented instead of unified. Banks can make the case for disciplined relationship lending and modest leverage because they are not being forced to chase volume. Life companies can still demand a premium for long-duration certainty because the long bond is doing some of that work for them. Debt funds can keep selling flexibility, speed and complexity capital because plenty of borrowers still cannot fit a pristine permanent-loan box. And CMBS remains open, but with the usual condition that the asset and the narrative both have to survive unforgiving underwriting.

You can see that in the week’s office-adjacent financing tape. Commercial Observer reported July 18 that Hudson Bay Capital provided a $60 million refinance for the Bell Works Fort Monmouth campus in Tinton Falls, New Jersey. The deal matters because it is not really a vote of confidence in generic office. It is a vote for a very specific kind of office-adjacent story: reuse, mixed-use character, and a tangible tenancy narrative, including Jersey Mike’s planned headquarters presence. That is the distinction lenders continue to make. Capital is not broadly saying yes to office. It is saying yes to office when the building has already moved meaningfully away from plain-vanilla office risk.

Trepp’s July 17 bank-lending work lines up with that same selective tone. Its latest analysis showed aggregate CRE loan growth improving, but the weakness is still concentrated at the largest banks, especially in construction. The median bank is still adding exposure, including in construction, while the biggest institutions remain the ones pulling balances down enough to drag the aggregate. That is a useful reality check because it keeps borrowers from overreading a few positive deals. There is credit out there, but it is not the same thing as broad reopening. Cleaner sponsorship, better basis, stronger deposits, and lower leverage still matter a lot if you are asking a bank to show up.

CMBS is sending a similarly mixed but usable signal. Trepp reported that the June special servicing rate rose 34 basis points to 11.20 percent, while its June delinquency report showed the headline delinquency rate fell 20 basis points to 7.35 percent. That combination is important. It says some loans are curing or resolving, but fresh stress is still moving into the workout channel. So securitization is available, yet it remains judgmental. The market is open, but it does not want hand-waving. If a borrower needs conduit execution, the deal still has to read cleanly from cash flow through rollover through refinanceability.

That discipline is one reason the lender stack today still looks pretty consistent. Banks want relationship business and cleaner stories. Life companies want stabilized assets and very little narrative drama. CMBS wants collateral that can travel through securitized underwriting without heroic assumptions. Debt funds want to be paid for speed, complexity or transitional business plans. None of that is new, but it remains the operating map because the curve and the credit data are not forcing a new hierarchy yet.

Multifamily is still the strongest lane, and this week’s flow backed that up from several angles at once. Commercial Observer reported July 18 that Ponce Bank supplied a $50 million construction loan for a 198-unit apartment project in Canarsie. The 485-x tax-abatement structure and affordable component matter here because they help explain why apartment construction can still clear when other projects stall. Construction capital is selective, but apartments with policy support, workable basis and a defined local demand story still have a path.

The affordable-housing capital story stayed active as well. Commercial Observer reported July 17 that Greystone Real Estate Capital closed a $137 million affordable housing development fund backed by low-income housing tax credit investors. The fund will support the development and preservation of nearly 2,000 units across 20 properties in nine states. That is not just an equity headline. It is a read on where conviction still exists. Institutional capital still wants affordable housing exposure, and that continues to support the parts of multifamily that come with mission alignment, durable subsidy structures and clearer policy support.

Agency execution also remains a stabilizer even when the freshest headline is not from this morning. Earlier this past week, Commercial Observer reported that Newmark provided $163 million of Fannie Mae-backed debt to refinance an 833-unit multifamily portfolio across Washington, D.C., Northern Virginia and Oregon. Even though that article sits outside the strict 24-hour window, it still helps frame the current lane because it is part of the same developing weekly pattern: agency debt remains one of the cleanest permanent-loan exits available for stabilized apartment collateral.

There is also a notable CMBS signal inside multifamily. Commercial Observer reported July 17 that Citi priced an $816.9 million all-multifamily conduit transaction made up of 27 five-year interest-only loans, the largest single-bank-contributed multifamily-only conduit deal since the global financial crisis. The AAA bonds priced at swaps plus 80 basis points, tighter than the comparable multifamily cash-flow execution earlier this year. That does not mean every apartment borrower suddenly has a wider-open securitized lane. But it does suggest that investors still want apartment collateral badly enough to support sharper execution when the pool is clean.

Trepp’s July 17 agency credit update reinforces that backdrop. Total securitized agency delinquency improved to 0.47 percent in May, with Fannie Mae at 0.24 percent, Freddie Mac at 0.87 percent and Ginnie Mae, FHA and HUD at 0.51 percent. Freddie still runs higher, but Trepp’s explanation is that structure and maturity treatment are still doing some of the work there rather than a broad deterioration in apartment credit. The bigger point is that multifamily credit performance inside the agency universe still looks steady enough to keep lenders comfortable.

On HUD and FHA specifically, I did not find a fresh multifamily execution or policy development published in the last 24 hours strong enough to lead as a standalone Sunday headline. But the Ginnie Mae, FHA and HUD delinquency reading still matters because it says the federally backed multifamily credit channel remains fundamentally stable, even if the newest visible momentum this week came more from banks, LIHTC equity, Fannie execution and apartment CMBS.

The concise markets snapshot this morning is this. The latest verified Treasury close is 4.18 percent on the 2-year, 4.28 percent on the 5-year, 4.55 percent on the 10-year and 5.06 percent on the 30-year. The latest verified SOFR print is 3.62 percent. Bank appetite is improving, but large banks are still not embracing construction risk in a broad way. Office financing exists mainly where a real reuse or tenancy story is already in place. CMBS is functioning, but still selective. Multifamily remains the deepest and cleanest pool for execution, especially where agencies, affordability structures or strong securitization fit are involved.

One thing to watch this week is whether the apartment capital stack keeps opening from multiple directions at once. If more multifamily-only CMBS, agency refinancings and affordable-housing capital raises print behind this week’s deals, then the read will be that lenders are getting more comfortable expanding around the strongest property type. If the follow-through is thin, then this week may end up looking more like concentration than reopening, with capital still clustering around the easiest collateral to defend.

The takeaway for this Sunday is straightforward. Nationally, the country is dealing with a cleanup story in Texas, a still-live environmental disruption story in the Northeast, a sharper federal enforcement story in Washington, and a new consumer health warning. In Debt Desk, the market is open, but it still demands specificity. Borrowers can get debt, but the cleanest executions are still going to assets lenders already trust, structures they can explain to committees, and stories they do not have to rescue after closing. That remains most true in multifamily, selectively true in repositioned office, and much less true anywhere the business plan depends on optimism carrying the underwriting.

Borrowers can get conduit execution, but only if the collateral and the story hold up under hard scrutiny.

The fresh bank-lending data adds another layer. Trepp published Friday that CRE loan growth is returning in parts of the market, but the softness is still concentrated at large banks, especially in construction. Owner-occupied and income-producing balances are growing in the aggregate, while construction balances remain held back by the biggest institutions. That is a useful read for borrowers because it fits what the market already feels like on the ground. Community and regional lenders can still show appetite in selective lanes, but the large-bank complex is not exactly throwing open the gates for development risk.

That is why the current lender stack still looks coherent. Banks want cleaner sponsorship, lower leverage and a relationship angle. Life companies want stabilized assets and low narrative risk, and they still expect to be paid for duration. CMBS wants assets that can survive securitized underwriting without heroic assumptions. Debt funds want to be compensated for flexibility, complexity and speed, and they are still winning assignments where the capital structure needs one of those three things.

Multifamily remains the strongest broad lane, and this week’s deals make that point from several directions at once. Commercial Observer reported Friday that Ponce Bank supplied a $50 million construction loan for a 198-unit apartment project in Brooklyn’s Canarsie neighborhood. The deal includes a 485-x tax-abatement angle and a partially affordable component, which is exactly the kind of structure that still helps construction financing come together in New York. The point is not that every apartment deal gets done. The point is that apartment construction still clears when sponsorship, basis and public-policy support line up.

Commercial Observer also reported Friday that Greystone closed a $137 million affordable housing development fund backed by institutional Low-Income Housing Tax Credit investors to support nearly 2,000 affordable housing units across 20 properties in nine states. That is not debt in the narrowest sense, but it matters directly to the financing environment because it shows institutional capital still wants exposure to the affordable-housing lane. In a market where pure equity acquisition volumes remain muted, affordable housing and tax-credit capital keep functioning as one of the cleaner ways to put money to work with mission and yield attached.

On the agency side, Commercial Observer reported earlier this week that Newmark provided $163 million of Fannie Mae-backed debt to refinance an 833-unit apartment portfolio spread across Washington, D.C., Northern Virginia and Oregon. That is another important signal. Agency debt is still one of the most dependable permanent-financing exits in the market, particularly for stabilized multifamily with institutional sponsorship. When borrowers can fit the box, the agencies still offer one of the clearest ways to replace shorter-term debt with longer-term certainty.

There is also a meaningful CMBS development in multifamily. Commercial Observer reported July 16 that Citi priced an $816.9 million multifamily-only conduit transaction made up of 27 five-year interest-only loans, the largest single-bank-contributed multifamily-only conduit deal since the global financial crisis. That is not just a bragging-rights headline. It suggests there is enough appetite for apartment collateral in securitized form to reopen a lane that had been relatively quiet. If that continues, it gives multifamily borrowers another outlet beyond banks, debt funds and the agencies.

Trepp’s latest agency credit data suggests that outlet is arriving against a still-healthy fundamental backdrop. Its July 17 report said total securitized agency delinquency improved to 0.47 percent in May, with Fannie Mae at 0.24 percent, Freddie Mac at 0.87 percent and Ginnie Mae, FHA and HUD at 0.51 percent. The Freddie number is higher, but Trepp’s point was that the divergence still looks more structural than credit-driven, with small-balance and retained matured-loan mechanics playing a role. The broader message is that agency apartment credit still looks strong, even in a higher-for-longer rate world.

HUD and FHA are quieter again on the fresh headline front. I did not find a new multifamily execution or policy update published within the last 24 hours strong enough to lead as a standalone Saturday item. That absence is itself part of the read. Publicly visible multifamily momentum this week came more from agencies, affordable-housing capital, banks willing to back apartment construction and securitized multifamily product than from a new HUD or FHA headline.

The concise markets snapshot this morning is this. The latest verified Treasury close is 4.18 percent on the 2-year, 4.28 percent on the 5-year, 4.55 percent on the 10-year and 5.06 percent on the 30-year. The latest verified SOFR print is 3.62 percent. Mortgage rates have moved back up to 6.55 percent. Office remains bifurcated, with capital still willing to engage where the reuse or tenancy story is concrete. CMBS is available but selective. Large banks remain cautious around construction. Multifamily continues to attract the broadest and cleanest lender interest, especially where affordability, agency eligibility or securitization fit the business plan.

One thing to watch next week is whether this week’s multifamily-only CMBS and agency headlines turn into a broader signal that the apartment capital stack is opening further, or whether they remain isolated examples of lenders favoring the safest collateral in a still-disciplined market. If more apartment executions print quickly behind Citi, Fannie and the affordable-housing capital flows, that will tell you lenders are getting more comfortable extending credit so long as the property type stays strong. If the follow-through is thin, then this week will read less like reopening and more like a reminder that capital is still clustering around the cleanest stories.

The takeaway for this Saturday is straightforward. Nationally, the country is heading into the weekend with live weather disruption, environmental strain and another round of political and legal friction. In Debt Desk, the market is still functioning, but it wants specificity. Borrowers can get debt. They just have to arrive with an asset class lenders already like, a structure lenders can defend and a story lenders do not have to rescue. That remains most true in multifamily, sometimes true in specialized or repurposed office, and still very much untrue for anything that depends on easy assumptions.

item.title: Debt Desk — Debt Desk Morning Brief for July 16, 2026
item.description: Texas flood danger, smoke and heat across the Midwest and Northeast, a fresh court clash in Seattle, and a politically charged White House address lead the national morning brief before Debt Desk turns to the latest verified Treasury and SOFR prints, CRE refinancing and construction activity, CMBS stress signals, multifamily capital flows, and one thing to watch for Thursday, July 16, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
It is Thursday, July 16th, and this is Debt Desk.

Let’s start with the national morning brief, because this morning the country feels like it is running through multiple stress tests at once. Some are weather stories, some are institutional stories, and some sit in that uncomfortable space where politics and operating risk start to bleed into each other.

The first story is South Texas, where flooding risk has become the immediate operating problem. The Associated Press updated Wednesday that heavy downpours washed out highways, stranded motorists and forced dozens of high-water rescues after some areas near the border with Mexico took up to a foot of rain. The National Weather Service warned that additional rounds of rain could create dangerous flash flooding into Thursday, and Governor Greg Abbott issued a disaster declaration covering dozens of counties. The reason this matters beyond weather is simple: repeated flooding does not just interrupt travel for a day. It hits local business activity, logistics, insurance expectations and public infrastructure all at once.

The second story is the smoke and heat combination spreading across the Midwest and Northeast. AP reported Wednesday that heavy wildfire smoke from Canada pushed unhealthy air deep into the U.S., while evacuations were underway in the Boundary Waters area of Minnesota and air-quality warnings stretched from Minnesota through Toronto into New York. That would be a meaningful story on its own, but it is colliding with a broad heat pattern that has already left large parts of the country running hotter than normal. When smoke and heat arrive together, the public-health risk changes. It is not just discomfort. It becomes a constraint on outdoor work, travel, tourism, schools, recreation and local emergency response.

The third story is a fresh institutional confrontation out of Seattle. AP reported that President Donald Trump fired the newly court-appointed top federal prosecutor in Seattle less than an hour after federal judges in the district unanimously appointed him. The immediate significance is narrow, but the larger signal is not. It is another example of how fights over appointments, legal authority and executive control are moving from background process stories into front-page operating stories. When that keeps happening, it affects how markets think about policy execution, litigation timelines and regulatory certainty.

The fourth story is tonight’s White House address. AP reported that Trump is expected to use a primetime address to focus on election issues and to revisit claims tied to past voting disputes. Whether the speech actually lands as a major policy moment or as another political provocation, the build-up matters. It tells you the administration wants election administration and election legitimacy back near the center of the national conversation heading toward the midterms. For investors and lenders, that does not price directly into debt costs this morning. But it does shape the broader volatility backdrop, especially if the speech triggers legal, legislative or state-level responses.

The fifth story is the immigration enforcement backlash building around the Department of Homeland Security. AP reported Wednesday that Trump said ICE should keep making traffic stops despite internal moves to limit them after a series of fatal encounters. That keeps the story alive because it is no longer just about a tragic set of incidents. It is also about whether agency leadership can change tactics when political pressure runs the other direction. For markets, that kind of friction matters because it becomes another measure of how consistently federal agencies can operate under pressure.

So the national setup this morning is a mix of physical disruption and political strain. Flooding is active in Texas. Smoke and heat are combining across a wider slice of the country. The White House is opening a new front in the election conversation. Immigration enforcement remains under scrutiny. And the fight over control of federal offices is getting more public, not less.

Now let’s turn to Debt Desk.

The first anchor, as always, is rates. As of this Thursday morning run, the latest verified official Treasury close is from Wednesday, July 15. The curve closed at 4.13 percent on the 2-year, 4.26 percent on the 5-year, 4.55 percent on the 10-year and 5.08 percent on the 30-year. The latest official SOFR print is 3.63 percent for Tuesday, July 14. Freddie Mac’s latest weekly primary mortgage market survey still shows the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate at 6.49 percent for the week ending July 9.

That curve tells a more useful story than the 10-year alone. The front end eased a bit with softer recent inflation data, but it is still high enough that floating-rate debt is not a casual choice. The 5-year remains the practical center of gravity for a lot of real borrower decisions, because it still offers a better pain trade than going all the way out the curve. And the 30-year staying above 5 percent keeps full-duration life company money expensive enough that many borrowers still prefer to compromise on tenor rather than pay for the longest lane.

In other words, the market is offering structure, not relief. Borrowers can get certainty, but they still have to choose carefully where they want to pay for it.

That is showing up in the latest deal flow. Commercial Observer reported July 15 that RXR, Waterfall Asset Management and New York Life provided $103 million for the recapitalization of Andalex Group’s Sylvan Corporate Center medical campus in Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey. It is not a plain office story and that is exactly why it matters. Capital is still showing clear preference for property types with stronger tenancy durability and more defensible demand. Medical office and healthcare-adjacent product continue to attract money because the cash-flow story is easier to underwrite than generic office.

The broader office lesson still comes from the divide inside the sector. Trepp’s July 14 analysis of what it called bifurcating office performance reinforced that capital is separating buildings that can still refinance from buildings that cannot. That lines up with the continuity story already on our tracker from Manhattan and Washington office financings earlier this week. Good offices are financeable. Proven turnarounds can reach permanent debt. But the market is still deeply skeptical of assets that have weak leasing, functional obsolescence or uncertain capex demands.

CMBS is open, but it is not forgiving. Trepp reported on July 13 that the CMBS special servicing rate rose 34 basis points in June to 11.20 percent, reversing the prior month’s decline, even as the June delinquency rate had separately improved to 7.35 percent. That combination is important. It says resolution is still happening, but stress is not gone. Some loans are curing, some are being worked through, and new trouble is still arriving. The headline for borrowers is that conduit execution exists, but scrutiny remains intense and spreads still need to compensate lenders for property-specific uncertainty.

That leaves the lender stack in a fairly coherent place this morning. Banks are lending, but still favoring relationship business, lower leverage and cleaner sponsorship stories. Life companies remain interested in stabilized, lower-leverage product, particularly when the borrower wants quality execution and can tolerate the cost of duration. CMBS is functioning best where the asset can survive securitized underwriting without too much narrative risk. Debt funds continue to fill the gap wherever the plan includes construction, lease-up, transition or some other complexity that traditional lenders would rather avoid.

The market is not closed. It is selective, disciplined and still charging heavily for ambiguity.

Multifamily remains the deepest lane, and the freshest visible evidence is still constructive. Commercial Observer reported July 15 that Slate Property Group and RiseBoro Community Partnership landed roughly $163 million of financing for two Williamsburg housing projects that will deliver 312 affordable apartments. That is a useful signal because it shows capital continuing to support affordable and mission-oriented apartment development even while broader construction lending remains selective. If a project has a strong public-policy angle, a defined takeout story and credible sponsorship, money can still line up.

There is another smaller but telling construction datapoint from Philadelphia. Commercial Observer reported July 14 that S3 Capital provided a $24 million construction loan to Ampere Capital Group for a 109-unit mixed-use apartment project in Fishtown. That is not a megadeal, but it helps confirm that debt funds are still active in the urban multifamily development lane where the sponsor, submarket and basis make sense. This is one of the clearest patterns in the market right now: banks are not absent, but nonbank lenders are still doing a lot of the work where flexibility matters.

And that fits the broader multifamily capital-markets story. Connect CRE reported July 15, citing Yardi Matrix, that private equity is increasingly using debt investments to gain apartment exposure because property sales remain relatively muted. The same report said debt funds are taking a bigger share of the market, agency lenders Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac have expanded securitization offerings, and multifamily-only CMBS pools are starting to come back. That is a concise description of how capital is adapting. If equity buyers do not love today’s pricing and rate backdrop, they can still express conviction through debt.

Agency activity remains one of the cleanest permanent-debt answers in the market. That was true earlier this week with the Northmarq Fannie Mae execution in Massachusetts and the Merchants Capital Freddie Mac affordable-housing deal in Kansas, and it remains true this morning as the broader tape develops. The agencies still look like the most dependable long-term debt lane for stabilized multifamily, especially where affordability, occupancy and sponsorship are easy to defend.

Freddie Mac’s own platform signals support that view. Its integrated Conventional Small product for loans under $10 million, announced this year, is another reminder that the agency wants to stay relevant across a wider borrower base, not just the largest institutional deals. Fannie Mae’s July-effective guide updates on insurance and servicing mechanics tell a similar story. These are not flashy headlines, but they are the sort of operating signals that matter when you are judging whether an origination channel is alive, current and still trying to reduce avoidable friction.

HUD and FHA are quieter again this morning. I did not find a fresh multifamily closing or policy headline from HUD or FHA published within the last 24 hours strong enough to carry as a primary item. So for now, the public tape remains more active around debt funds, local construction lenders and the agencies than around HUD-led multifamily execution.

The multifamily CMBS story is also worth keeping in frame. Apartments still price better than office in conduit markets, but that does not mean apartment underwriting is loose. The market still prefers in-place occupancy, realistic expense assumptions and business plans that do not depend on heroic rent growth. Borrowers who bought into aggressive value-add assumptions a few years ago still face real refinance friction even in the strongest property type.

The concise markets snapshot this morning is this. The latest verified Treasury close is 4.13 percent on the 2-year, 4.26 percent on the 5-year, 4.55 percent on the 10-year and 5.08 percent on the 30-year. The latest verified SOFR print is 3.63 percent. Mortgage rates remain high enough that housing turnover stays constrained, which still supports rental demand even if rent growth is modest. Healthcare-oriented commercial assets are still finding lender support. Office remains bifurcated. CMBS is open but judgmental. Debt funds are still solving for construction and transition risk. And agency multifamily debt remains one of the cleanest lanes in the market.

One thing to watch today is whether the recent move lower in the front end of the Treasury curve actually changes borrower behavior or just makes existing preferences more obvious. If the 2-year keeps easing while the 30-year stays stubbornly high, that still argues for five- to seven-year fixed-rate structures as the most practical compromise. If that dynamic holds, life companies should stay selective, banks should keep protecting proceeds, CMBS should remain disciplined on spreads, and debt funds should continue to win the assignments where certainty and flexibility matter more than price alone.

The takeaway for this Thursday is straightforward. Nationally, the country is dealing with active weather disruption, environmental stress and another round of institutional conflict. In Debt Desk, capital is present, but it still expects borrowers to arrive with clarity. Multifamily remains the strongest financing lane, especially where affordability and stabilization are easy to prove. CMBS is functioning, though hardly loose. Office is still a tale of two markets. And the curve continues to say the same thing it has been saying for weeks: structure matters, duration is expensive, and there is still no free money in this market.

item.title: Debt Desk — Debt Desk Morning Brief for July 13, 2026
item.description: A dangerous U.S. heat wave, Missouri flood rescues, a sharp press-freedom clash, and election-administration uncertainty lead the national morning brief before Debt Desk turns to the latest Treasury and SOFR prints, office and multifamily financings, CMBS execution tone, agency signals, and one thing to watch for Monday, July 13, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
It is Monday, July 13th, and this is Debt Desk.

Let’s start with the national morning brief, because the country is opening the week with a familiar pattern: the biggest stories are operating stories. They affect how people move, how agencies function and how risk gets priced.

The first story this morning is the heat. The Associated Press first published on Saturday, July 11, and updated on Sunday, July 12, that a widespread and dangerous heat wave is pressing across much of the United States under a strong heat dome, with triple-digit temperatures in parts of the West and Plains before the system pushes farther east. AP reported that more than 90 local temperature records could be tied or broken through midweek, with many of those records on the overnight side. That matters because hot nights turn the story into a stress test for power systems, outdoor labor, public health operations, logistics and household budgets.

The second story is flood damage and emergency response in Missouri. AP first published on Saturday, July 11, and updated that story over the weekend after floodwaters forced helicopter rescues from a summer camp, left one woman dead, and shut down roads as the Black River continued rising. It is another reminder that climate and catastrophe risk keep moving from tail event toward regular operating backdrop, which matters for insurers, municipal issuers, utilities and lenders underwriting local durability.

The third story is still the administration’s pressure campaign against the press. AP first published on Friday, July 11, and updated over the weekend that the Department of Justice subpoenaed New York Times reporters over their reporting on security concerns tied to the Qatari-gifted Air Force One. The article says the subpoenas would force testimony before a federal grand jury in Manhattan this week. For markets, this is another sign that information risk, legal process risk and reputational risk are increasingly entangled.

The fourth story is election administration. AP published on Friday, July 10, that President Donald Trump removed Democratic members of the Election Assistance Commission, the federal body that helps distribute election grants, test voting systems and maintain the national voter registration form. That is an important story not because markets trade every agency staffing move, but because this one bears directly on how a critical national process is administered ahead of the midterms. If legal challenges or appointment delays keep the commission unstable, then grants, certifications and procedural confidence all become more fragile. This is exactly the kind of institutional story that can stay in the background right up until some practical deadline makes it suddenly important.

The fifth story is the national housing backdrop. Freddie Mac’s weekly mortgage survey, released Thursday, July 9, put the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate at 6.49 percent. AP’s housing coverage from Friday, July 11, also pointed to slowing existing-home sales and a record median home price. That still leaves turnover constrained and affordability stressed, which is one reason multifamily demand still has structural support.

So that is the national setup for Monday morning. A large swath of the country is overheating, parts of the Midwest are cleaning up from flood rescues, the federal government is escalating a confrontation with major news organizations, election administration is looking less settled than it should, and housing affordability still is not easing in a meaningful way. None of that shuts the market. But all of it adds friction.

Now let’s turn to Debt Desk.

The first anchor, as always, is rates. As of this Monday morning run, the latest official Treasury close available is from Friday, July 10. The U.S. Treasury curve closed at 4.21 percent on the 2-year, 4.30 percent on the 5-year, 4.56 percent on the 10-year and 5.06 percent on the 30-year. The latest official SOFR print available from the New York Fed is 3.53 percent for Thursday, July 9. Freddie Mac’s average 30-year mortgage rate, again for the week ending July 9, is 6.49 percent.

That is still a workable market, but it is not an easy one. The front end remains high enough that floating-rate debt still needs to be justified, not defaulted into. A 3.53 SOFR print does not sound terrible in isolation, but once spread, cap cost, reserves and extension assumptions are layered in, the carry is still meaningful. The 2-year Treasury tells you floating money is not cheap enough to be casual. The 5-year tells you why so much real fixed-rate execution keeps clustering in the middle of the curve. And the 30-year tells you why long-duration life company money remains expensive enough that only certain borrowers truly want it.

Looking only at the 10-year misses too much. Many actual borrower decisions are being made somewhere between the 2-year and the 7-year, with the 5-year acting as the practical center of gravity. The curve is not telling borrowers that all-in debt is attractive. It is telling them that the middle lanes remain the least painful.

The clearest large office refinancing datapoint still comes from Manhattan. JLL announced on Thursday, July 9, that it arranged a $352 million floating-rate SASB refinancing for 425 Lexington Avenue through Goldman Sachs, fully pre-placed with funds and accounts managed by BlackRock. That is an important transaction because it says institutional office liquidity is absolutely there for the right product, but also that the market is still highly selective about what counts as financeable office. This is a 99 percent leased, heavily upgraded, Grand Central-adjacent tower. In other words, this is not a generic office reopening story. It is a proof-of-liquidity story for elite collateral.

That deal matters beyond one tower because it shows how execution is happening. The financing was curated, structured and pre-placed with serious institutional capital. If the building is first-rate, the tenant story is strong and the sponsor is credible, large office debt can get done. If those elements weaken, the market becomes much thinner very quickly.

There is also a smaller but useful office CMBS signal from Washington. Commercial Observer reported on Friday, July 10, that Jemal Equities refinanced 1750 H Street NW with a $27 million CMBS loan from Citibank arranged by Meridian Capital Group. That building was almost fully vacant when Jemal bought it in July 2025, but the report says it saw leasing momentum strong enough to take out the bridge debt with fixed-rate permanent financing. That matters because it shows the conduit market is still willing to finance office outside the absolute trophy tier when a real leasing story has already been proven. The takeaway is not that office has become easy. The takeaway is that office can still move from transitional to permanent capital if execution risk has already been burned down.

That lines up with the broader CMBS backdrop. Trepp reported on July 10 that the June CMBS delinquency rate fell 20 basis points to 7.35 percent, helped by a large lodging cure. Trepp’s recent conduit analysis makes the more useful point: five-year conduit loans have become the market’s default setting, while spreads remain disciplined and office still prices wider than multifamily.

So the CMBS read this morning is fairly straightforward. The market is open. It is functioning. It is not in retreat. But it is rewarding discipline, medium-duration structures and collateral quality. Borrowers who still think the conduit market is back in its old form are reading the tape incorrectly.

That brings us to execution tone across the lender stack. Banks are still in the market, but they remain selective on leverage, sponsorship and relationship value. Life companies remain credible for stabilized, lower-leverage product, but a 30-year Treasury north of 5 percent means that duration comes at a visible cost. CMBS is working where the asset can survive securitized scrutiny. Debt funds remain the flexibility providers wherever the assignment includes construction, lease-up or recapitalization complexity.

In other words, the capital stack has breadth, but not much tolerance for ambiguity. The market is not closed. It is judgmental.

Multifamily remains the deepest lane in that stack, and the freshest headline there is still the July 10 Dwight Mortgage Trust construction loan in Gilroy, California. Connect CRE reported that Dwight provided a $183 million construction loan for a 530-unit multifamily development, the largest construction financing in the company’s history. That is a significant debt-fund signal. It shows that apartment construction is still one of the few property types capable of attracting large-scale floating-rate development capital when the sponsor, submarket and affordability profile make sense. The deal includes both market-rate townhomes and income-restricted units, which matters because mixed-income and workforce-oriented stories continue to align better with today’s capital preferences than purely speculative luxury development.

That Dwight financing also says something broader about where risk is being warehoused. Banks have pulled back from many construction assignments. Debt funds have not disappeared from the lane. They have simply gotten more selective and more expensive.

Agency activity remains one of the cleanest permanent-debt answers for stabilized apartments. Connect CRE’s July 9 report on Northmarq’s $22.855 million Fannie Mae DUS acquisition financing for Elora Flats and Townhomes in Lawrence, Massachusetts is still worth carrying because it captures the tone of the agency market very well. The deal came with a seven-year term and four years of interest-only payments on a property that was 100 percent mission-driven and had maintained high occupancy. That is exactly the kind of file the agencies can still handle with confidence: steady cash flow, clear affordability profile, proven performance, and a structure that gives the borrower enough breathing room without pretending leverage is free.

Freddie Mac also remains visibly active, even when the public tape is showing more policy than closings. Freddie Mac Multifamily published its insurance update on July 7, describing changes meant to align requirements and improve consistency. That is not a splashy financing announcement, but it matters operationally. When agency platforms are refining insurance standards instead of freezing them, that is a sign that the machine is active, current and still trying to reduce avoidable friction for borrowers and servicers.

On the Freddie closing side, Connect CRE reported on July 9 that Merchants Capital secured a $10.8 million Freddie Mac Unfunded Forward TEL loan for Floret Hill, a 121-unit affordable housing development in Lawrence, Kansas. That is a smaller transaction than the Dwight construction headline, but it is useful because it shows Freddie still has a clear lane in affordable multifamily execution, especially where public support, tax credit equity and agency debt fit together in a coherent capital stack.

Fannie Mae’s own guide updates remain part of the story too. The Multifamily Guide shows Guide Update 26-16 on insurance became effective July 6. Again, that is not the kind of item you lead a show with, but for active borrowers and lenders it is exactly the kind of operational signal that says agency channels remain open and engaged.

HUD and FHA are quieter again this morning. I did not find a fresh multifamily closing or policy development from HUD or FHA published within the last 24 hours strong enough to carry as a lead item. That means the visible momentum on the public tape right now is sitting more with debt funds and the agencies than with HUD-driven headlines.

The multifamily CMBS read is also worth a quick note. Apartments still price better than office in the conduit market, and Trepp’s spread work makes that clear, but multifamily is not frictionless. Older value-add assumptions, tighter refinance proceeds and higher operating costs still complicate takeouts for some borrowers. So yes, apartment remains the most financeable major property type. But even here, the market is rewarding in-place cash flow and realistic leverage more than optimistic underwriting.

The concise markets snapshot this morning is this. The latest official Treasury close is 4.21 percent on the 2-year, 4.30 percent on the 5-year, 4.56 percent on the 10-year and 5.06 percent on the 30-year. The latest official SOFR print is 3.53 percent. Freddie Mac’s 30-year mortgage average is 6.49 percent. Trophy office can refinance if the asset is undeniably strong. Select office CMBS deals can still clear. Five-year conduit structures remain the market’s default format. Debt funds are still winning meaningful multifamily construction assignments. Agency permanent debt remains one of the cleanest ways through the market for stabilized apartment collateral.

One thing to watch this week is whether more borrowers continue choosing the middle of the curve rather than either floating longer or paying up for full duration. If the 5-year Treasury stays well inside the 30-year and SOFR remains sticky, then five- to seven-year fixed-rate executions should keep looking like the most rational compromise in the market. If that dynamic holds, expect life companies to stay selective, CMBS to keep favoring medium-duration structures, banks to protect proceeds, and debt funds to remain the solution set for more dynamic business plans.

The takeaway for this Monday is simple. Nationally, the country is starting the week with heat stress, flood damage, institutional friction and stubborn housing costs. In Debt Desk, capital is available, but it still charges for uncertainty. Office debt is open for the best buildings and for select proven turnarounds. Multifamily remains the strongest lane, especially where affordability, occupancy and sponsorship are easy to defend. The agencies are active. Debt funds matter. And the curve is still telling borrowers that structure matters more than hope.

It also adds to the broader sense that policy, litigation and headline risk are becoming harder to separate.

Freddie Mac’s weekly survey, released Thursday, put the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate at 6.49 percent for the week ending July 9. Put together, that is still the same uncomfortable national equation: activity is sluggish, borrowing costs are elevated, but prices remain high enough to keep affordability badly strained. For this audience, that is not just a single-family story. It is one of the core reasons multifamily demand remains durable and why apartment finance continues to command more lender attention than most other property types.

There is also a macro layer beneath that housing story. AP’s America In Focus package, published Friday, July 11, said Federal Reserve officials remain divided on where inflation is headed next. That matters because it keeps borrowers from assuming easy rate relief is right around the corner. If inflation still looks arguable from inside the Fed, then financing markets will keep pricing caution.

So the national setup this morning is fairly straightforward. The country is dealing with an extreme heat event, a new fight over press protections, deeper election-administration conflict and a housing market that is still too expensive for comfort. None of those stories shut down capital flows on their own. Together, they reinforce a backdrop where uncertainty keeps getting layered into everyday operating decisions.

Now let’s turn to Debt Desk.

The first anchor, as always, is rates. I verified the latest official Treasury close available as of this Sunday run, which means Friday, July 10. The curve closed at 4.21 percent on the 2-year, 4.30 percent on the 5-year, 4.56 percent on the 10-year and 5.06 percent on the 30-year. I also verified through the New York Fed that the latest official SOFR print is 3.53 percent for Thursday, July 9.

That still looks like an open market, but not a forgiving one. The front end remains high enough that floating-rate debt cannot be treated casually. A 3.53 SOFR print sounds manageable only until lender spread, reserves, cap costs and extension risk are layered on top. The 5-year Treasury at 4.30 remains one of the most important numbers on the screen because it sits near the part of the curve where a lot of real executions are actually clearing. Borrowers who want certainty but do not want to pay full long-bond freight keep getting pulled into that middle lane. Then you get to the 30-year at 5.06, and that is where life-company money can still make sense, but mostly for clean stories that truly want duration and can live with disciplined leverage.

The broader Treasury shape matters too. Looking only at the 10-year misses too much of the real financing math. The 2-year tells you what floating debt still costs to carry. The 5-year tells you where practical fixed-rate negotiations are landing. The 30-year tells you why full-duration money is available but expensive. That is why the curve continues to argue for specificity rather than optimism. Borrowers are being rewarded for picking the right lane, not for hoping all lanes get cheaper.

The freshest large office financing datapoint remains the refinancing of 425 Lexington Avenue in Midtown Manhattan. JLL announced on Thursday, July 9, that it arranged a $352 million floating-rate SASB refinancing for Vanbarton Group through Goldman Sachs, with the loan pre-placed entirely with funds and accounts managed by BlackRock. That is a meaningful transaction because it says two things at once. First, institutional office liquidity still exists for the right tower, in the right location, with the right tenancy and sponsorship. Second, the execution path is highly curated. This is not evidence that generic office is suddenly easy. It is evidence that top-tier office can still clear when the capital-markets machinery is lined up properly from the start.

There is also a smaller but useful office CMBS signal from Washington. Commercial Observer published Friday, July 10, that Jemal Equities refinanced 1750 H Street NW with a $27 million CMBS loan from Citibank that Meridian Capital Group arranged. That matters because it shows conduit-style office execution is still alive beyond the trophy tier. The market will finance performing office when leasing momentum, debt yield and sponsorship line up. But it still wants proof. CMBS is available. It is just not generous.

That fits the broader securitized backdrop. Trepp reported on July 10 that the June CMBS delinquency rate improved by 20 basis points to 7.35 percent. That is directionally constructive, especially after a stretch where distress headlines were doing most of the talking. At the same time, Trepp’s recent spread work says five-year conduit loans have effectively become the market’s default setting, with median 2026 office spreads still running wider than multifamily and a touch wider than the overall conduit market. That is the key nuance. Sentiment is better. Execution is functioning. But office still pays a premium for scrutiny, and medium-duration structures remain the practical clearing point for a lot of securitized borrowing.

That leads directly into lender tone across the capital stack. Banks are still lending, but mainly where the file is simple, the relationship matters, or the asset is plainly financeable. Life companies remain credible for stabilized, lower-leverage product, but the 30-year Treasury above 5 percent keeps them selective. CMBS is open for assets that can withstand securitized underwriting. Debt funds remain the flexibility provider where the assignment includes construction risk, lease-up, heavy repositioning or any story that falls outside a conventional box. In other words, the market has breadth. What it does not have is much patience for ambiguity.

Multifamily remains the deepest financing lane, and the freshest headline there came Friday evening from Connect CRE. Dwight Mortgage Trust provided a $183 million construction loan for a 530-unit luxury multifamily development in Gilroy, California, which Connect described as the largest construction financing in Dwight’s history. That is a strong signal for the apartment market because it shows debt funds are still very much willing to take development risk when the scale, sponsorship and submarket story are compelling enough. Construction lending has not disappeared. It has become selective, and multifamily is still the property type most likely to earn a real yes.

Agency execution is still visible as well, even if the public tape is quieter than the debt-fund lane. Connect CRE’s July 9 report on Northmarq’s $22.855 million Fannie Mae DUS acquisition financing for Elora Flats and Townhomes in Lawrence, Massachusetts remains relevant because it is exactly the kind of deal that keeps showing where the floor of the market is. Stable apartment collateral with a sensible leverage profile can still move through the agency machine cleanly. The structure there, a seven-year term with four years of interest-only, also reinforces the point that the market is still rewarding borrowers who want practical certainty more than maximum leverage.

The official agency signals support that read. Freddie Mac Multifamily published an insurance update on Monday, July 7, describing changes that reduce some required umbrella limits and simplify insurer-rating requirements, which is a small but useful sign that the platform is still trying to keep execution workable for borrowers and lenders. Fannie Mae’s Multifamily Guide shows Guide Update 26-16 on insurance became effective July 6. Those are not headline deal announcements, but they do matter. They say the agencies remain current, active and operational, which is exactly what borrowers want from their most dependable permanent-debt channels.

HUD and FHA are quieter again this morning. I did not find a fresh multifamily deal closing or policy bulletin from HUD or FHA published within the last 24 hours, and I did not find a Friday development strong enough to lead the section. That absence is itself informative. Right now, the visible momentum is sitting with debt funds and the agencies, while HUD remains more of a background option than the center of the public conversation. If long-duration fixed rates stay expensive and borrowers keep prioritizing proceeds and certainty, HUD can come back into focus quickly. But as of this run, it is not the lane setting the tone.

The multifamily CMBS conversation also deserves a quick note. Apartment still prices materially better than office in conduit land, but it is not immune from refinancing friction. Loans originated under lower-rate assumptions still face proceeds pressure, and that means even good apartment collateral can require more borrower equity or more structuring discipline than sponsors expected a couple of years ago. Multifamily remains the best neighborhood in the market. It is just not a frictionless one.

The concise markets snapshot this morning is this. The official Friday, July 10 Treasury close was 4.21 percent on the 2-year, 4.30 percent on the 5-year, 4.56 percent on the 10-year and 5.06 percent on the 30-year. The latest official SOFR print is 3.53 percent for July 9. Freddie Mac’s average 30-year mortgage rate is 6.49 percent for the week ending July 9. Institutional office can still refinance when the asset quality is undeniable. CMBS remains open, but medium-duration structures are doing a lot of the work. Debt funds are still winning apartment construction assignments. Agency multifamily execution remains one of the cleanest permanent-debt lanes in the market.

One thing to watch this week is whether borrowers keep moving toward the middle of the curve instead of either floating indefinitely or paying up for maximum duration. If the 5-year Treasury stays materially inside the 30-year and SOFR remains sticky, five- to seven-year fixed-rate executions may keep looking like the market’s most rational compromise. If that continues, expect life companies to stay selective, banks to protect proceeds, CMBS to keep favoring disciplined structures and debt funds to remain the main solution set wherever the business plan is still dynamic.

The takeaway for this Sunday is simple. Nationally, the country is running hotter, more expensive and more litigious. In Debt Desk, capital is available, but it still charges for uncertainty. Trophy office can clear. Select office CMBS can clear. Multifamily remains the strongest financing story, especially when the collateral is clean or the development thesis is convincing. Agencies are open. Debt funds are important. And the rate curve is still telling borrowers to stop waiting for a perfect setup and start matching duration to what they can actually carry.
